title: Montana’s plan to become an experimental medical hub just pushed forward

solution_concreteness.evidence: Montana’s latest right-to-try legislation is unique. While other jurisdictions with similar laws limit access to drugs to people with terminal illness, in Montana access is theoretically available to anyone who gives informed consent and can pay. The state’s Department of Health and Human Services recently finalized rules to implement the law. The rules stipulate that patient consumers provide fully informed consent and that each application be reviewed by a board that includes a Montana-certified doctor, expert scientists, and an ethicist.

systemic_impact.evidence: Montana’s plan to become an experimental medical hub just pushed forward. The state’s effort to expand the “right to try” is making headway, and the first drugs are about to be reviewed. As of this week in Montana, any biotech company with an experimental drug has a clear path to selling it to consumers.

evidence_strength.evidence: Supporters of the law stress that they want the process to be responsible. “It will be done in a very rigorous way, with qualified medical professionals and appropriate oversight,” says Matt Kaeberlein, a scientist on the first board, which was formed independently of the state health department. But other experts are worried about the potential for harm in selling unproven treatments to people without oversight from the US Food and Drug Administration. “I would be concerned,” says Aaron Kesselheim, a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School with expertise in health policy and drug regulation.

governance_intervention_strength.evidence: Montana’s latest right-to-try legislation is unique. While other jurisdictions with similar laws limit access to drugs to people with terminal illness, in Montana access is theoretically available to anyone who gives informed consent and can pay. The state’s Department of Health and Human Services recently finalized rules to implement the law. The rules stipulate that patient consumers provide fully informed consent and that each application be reviewed by a board that includes a Montana-certified doctor, expert scientists, and an ethicist.

equity_access.evidence: in Montana access is theoretically available to anyone who gives informed consent and can pay. That includes people desperate for treatments for rare diseases. It also includes those who are interested in longevity and want to try out drugs pitched as preventive therapies.

economic_viability.evidence: Companies whose drugs have been through preliminary testing—sometimes in as few as 10 healthy people—can pay $12,500 to apply to a newly established review board for approval. Once its treatment is rubber-stamped, the company can set the price of the drug and sell it via experimental treatment clinics, the first of which is likely to be up and running around the end of this year.

title: Major change to passport renewals rolls out across Canada. Here’s how it works

solution_concreteness.evidence: The Canadian government has announced that online passport renewal is now available to all eligible adult Canadians in Canada. The rollout follows a pilot program introduced in December 2024, which previously limited online passport renewals to a maximum of 2,000 applications per day. With the trial now complete, that daily cap has been removed.

systemic_impact.evidence: online passport renewal is now available to all eligible adult Canadians in Canada

evidence_strength.evidence: Announcing the expansion on Tuesday, immigration minister Lena Diab said: “Expanding online renewal gives eligible Canadians a simpler, more convenient way to renew their passports, without unnecessary barriers or delays. This is part of the Government of Canada’s ongoing work to modernize passport services and deliver public services that are responsive to the needs of Canadians today.”

governance_intervention_strength.evidence: The change builds on other recent improvements to passport services, including an online application status tracker and a guarantee that applications will be processed within 30 business days or the passport is free. Both of these measures also apply to online renewal applications.

equity_access.evidence: Online renewals are currently only available for Canadians whose home and mailing address are in Canada. Canadians applying for their passport outside Canada can do so by mail or by visiting a Government of Canada office abroad. The online renewal process is also limited to Canadians whose passport is set to expire within six months or has already expired. Currently, only adult Canadians are eligible, but Diab said she hasn’t ruled out the possibility of further expanding the online application system to include children under 16 and Canadians applying abroad in the future.

economic_viability.evidence: The cost of renewing a passport online is the same as completing the process in person. A five-year adult passport costs $122.50, a 10-year adult passport costs $163.50, and a child passport (age 0 to 15) costs $58.50. Canadian passport fees increased in March this year for the first time since 2013, and are now subject to the Services Fees Act (SFA), a law that requires fee decreases or increases to be based on inflation. As a result, passport fees rose by 2.7 per cent earlier this year.
